q: Trace the Wachau's regulatory independence: what is Vinea Wachau, what does its Codex forbid, and what changed with the 2020 vintage?
accept: vinea wachau 1983 private association, codex bans chaptalization and concentration, wachau dac from 2020
codex wachau forbids enrichment concentration and aromatization; wachau became a dac in 2020
private growers association with a purity codex, steinfeder federspiel smaragd are trademarks, dac from the 2020 vintage
vinea wachau nobilis districtus codex, plus the wachau dac origin pyramid since 2020
ans: Vinea Wachau Nobilis Districtus, founded in 1983, is a private growers' association, not an appellation body. Its Codex Wachau binds members to fruit grown in the Wachau alone and forbids enrichment (chaptalization), concentration, aromatization and additives such as oak chips — a purity pledge stricter than any French or German law. Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd are its trademarks, not legal categories, and they rank ripeness, not site. With the 2020 vintage the region finally entered the national system as Wachau DAC, adopting the Gebietswein–Ortswein–Riedenwein origin pyramid. The two now run in parallel: origin from the DAC, style and ripeness from Vinea Wachau.
exp: For decades the Wachau argued that a private code of practice policed quality better than appellation law, and on winemaking it did. What it could not do privately was protect origin language — Ried and village names. The DAC supplied exactly that, which is why the region joined without giving up its trademarks. The candidate's takeaway: on a Wachau label the ripeness word and the origin word come from two different rulebooks.

q: Compare the three DACs whose reds are defined by Blaufränkisch — Leithaberg, Mittelburgenland and Eisenberg — on soil, climate and resulting style.
accept: leithaberg limestone and schist taut, mittelburgenland clay loam ripe and broad, eisenberg iron slate lean and peppery
limestone schist versus heavy clay versus iron-rich slate, cool to warm to cool again
leithaberg mineral and saline, mittelburgenland warm and full, eisenberg ferrous and peppery
leithaberg on the leithagebirge, mittelburgenland blaufrankischland clay, eisenberg slate in the south
ans: Leithaberg sits on the limestone and mica-schist of the Leithagebirge above the Neusiedlersee, its reds at least 85% Blaufränkisch: taut, saline, cool-fruited and the most mineral of the three (it is also the one DAC of the three with a white wine, from Grüner Veltliner, Weissburgunder, Chardonnay and Neuburger). Mittelburgenland — the Blaufränkischland — is deep, heavy clay-loam in the warmest Pannonian pocket, sheltered on three sides: dark, ripe, broad-shouldered wines, historically the most oaked. Eisenberg, in the cooler, wetter far south, is iron-rich loam over slate and green schist: the leanest and most peppery, with a ferrous, herbal edge and lower alcohol. One grape, three readings.
exp: Blaufränkisch is a natural cross of Blaue Zimmettraube and Weisser Heunisch (Gouais Blanc) — no relation to Pinot or Gamay — and it is Lemberger in Germany, Kékfrankos in Hungary. It buds early and ripens very late, so heat and the soil's water-holding capacity dominate its style more than winemaking does; that is exactly why three DACs for one grape is not redundancy but a soil map. Each of the three requires a minimum of 85% Blaufränkisch. A candidate who adds Rosalia DAC, created for the 2017 vintage, is right to: it also bottles varietal Blaufränkisch, but shares the stage with Zweigelt rather than being built on Blaufränkisch alone.

q: How does the word 'Reserve' function on an Austrian DAC label, and what does it require?
accept: reserve is a style term needing minimum 13 percent alcohol, klassik is the lighter dry style
13% abv minimum and later release, may show wood and botrytis unlike klassik
weinviertel klassik 12 percent, reserve 13 percent, a style term that runs beside origin
reserve marks ripeness and 13 percent alcohol, independent of the gebiets orts ried pyramid
ans: Reserve is a style designation, not an origin: it marks the riper, fuller, later-released end of a DAC's range and requires a minimum of 13% alcohol. Where the lighter style — 'Klassik' in the DACs that use the term — must be fresh, dry and free of obvious wood or botrytis character, a Reserve is permitted both. Weinviertel DAC is the model: Klassik at minimum 12% alcohol, peppery and unoaked; Weinviertel DAC Reserve at minimum 13%, released later. Crucially, Reserve runs on a separate axis from origin, so a wine can be an Ortswein or a Riedenwein and a Reserve at the same time.
exp: This is the point candidates miss: Austrian labels carry origin and style on two independent axes, unlike Germany where the origin tier and the ripeness word were historically tangled. Reserve also has real commercial force — it is where oak and botrytis notes are legally allowed to appear in a DAC wine that would otherwise be rejected by the tasting panel for atypicity.

q: Move east from the Wachau along the Danube: characterise Kremstal, Kamptal, Traisental and Wagram by soil and signature.
accept: kremstal loess and gneiss, kamptal loess plus heiligenstein sandstone, traisental limestone conglomerate, wagram deep loess and roter veltliner
loess at kremstal and wagram, heiligenstein in the kamptal, conglomerate limestone in the traisental
traisental is limestone conglomerate, wagram is the loess plateau of roter veltliner
kremstal krems senftenberg, kamptal langenlois heiligenstein, traisental limestone, wagram loess
ans: Kremstal, around Krems, is the broadest — loess terraces east of the town for Grüner Veltliner, primary rock and gneiss upstream at Senftenberg for Riesling. Kamptal follows the Kamp north from Langenlois: loess again for Grüner, and the Zöbinger Heiligenstein's Permian desert sandstone with volcanic conglomerate for its greatest Rieslings. Traisental, on the south bank, is the smallest and the most distinctive geologically — limestone conglomerate that gives Grüner a chalky, herb-edged cut (Huber, Neumayer). Wagram is a vast loess plateau on the north bank east of Kremstal, giving powerful, broad Grüner, and it is the home of Roter Veltliner (Ott, Leth); its southern arm reaches Klosterneuburg at Vienna's edge, and it was the last of the four to become a DAC.
exp: The Danube regions are usually blurred together as 'Grüner country', but each has one fact that identifies it in an oral: Heiligenstein for the Kamptal, limestone conglomerate for the Traisental, Roter Veltliner and loess depth for the Wagram, and the loess/primary-rock split for the Kremstal. Roter Veltliner in particular is a trap — unrelated to Grüner Veltliner, and almost entirely confined to the Wagram.
